rules.name: Hook truncates or drops the model's own relation
rules.short_description: A hook runs TRUNCATE or DROP on the model's own relation.
rules.long_description:
A hook that truncates or drops the model's relation can remove data before a replacement succeeds. A post-hook can remove the result of a successful build. Failure recovery depends on the adapter and statement. Do not assume the hook and model share a transaction on Snowflake.

The rule reports `TRUNCATE` or `DROP` in a hook that targets `{{ this }}` or the model's own relation. A table materialization already rebuilds its result on each run.

References:
- [pre-hook & post-hook](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/resource-configs/pre-hook-post-hook)
- [Materializations](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/materializations)
- [Configure incremental models](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/incremental-models)
rules.remediation: Remove the hook if the materialization can perform the required rebuild. Use `materialized='table'` for a full replacement. For changed rows, choose a supported incremental strategy and define its filter and key requirements. Check first-run and full-refresh behavior before replacing the existing load.

examples.title: Truncate in a hook
examples.bad:
{{ config(pre_hook='truncate table {{ this }}') }}
select * from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}
examples.good:
{{ config(materialized='table') }}
select * from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}

rules.name: Hook deletes rows from the model relation
rules.short_description: A hook deletes rows from the model's relation and may also reference another model.
rules.long_description:
A separate delete hook can remove rows without a successful replacement. On adapters such as Postgres and Redshift, hooks can share the model transaction. Do not assume this behavior on Snowflake.

The rule reports a hook that deletes from the model's own relation. It notes a `ref()` call in the hook. A `ref()` can establish a dependency; the hook write does not become a separate model output.

Use a supported incremental strategy when its row-replacement behavior matches the intended delete. `delete+insert` replaces rows for incoming keys. It does not mean arbitrary row deletion or partition replacement. A standard `merge` does not delete a row merely because a soft-delete flag is present.

References:
- [pre-hook & post-hook](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/resource-configs/pre-hook-post-hook)
- [About incremental strategy](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/incremental-strategy)
- [About ref function](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/dbt-jinja-functions/ref)
rules.remediation: Check the delete predicate and incoming keys before changing the load. Use `delete+insert` or `merge` only when the supported strategy produces the same result. If the model retains a soft-delete flag, define how consumers use it. If physical deletion is required, implement and test that behavior explicitly.

examples.title: Delete in a hook
examples.bad:
{{ config(post_hook='delete from {{ this }} where load_date = current_date()') }}
select * from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}
examples.good:
{{ config(materialized='incremental', incremental_strategy='delete+insert', unique_key='order_id') }}
select * from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}

rules.name: Folder hook changes data once per model
rules.short_description: A folder pre-hook or post-hook runs TRUNCATE, DELETE, INSERT, or CALL for each model that inherits it.
rules.long_description:
A folder hook applies to each model that inherits it, not once to the whole run. If these hooks change shared data, later or concurrent models can undo earlier work. The effect depends on the statement and target.

The rule reports folder `+pre-hook` or `+post-hook` entries with `TRUNCATE`, `DELETE`, or `INSERT`. It reports `CALL` at information level. The level rises to warning when the project contains `SSC-EWI-INF0039` or `SSC-EWI-INF0038`. This escalation is a local migration check.

Run-level hooks are an option for once-per-command work. They can also run for commands such as `dbt compile` and `dbt test`; moving a destructive statement there needs review.

References:
- [pre-hook & post-hook](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/resource-configs/pre-hook-post-hook)
- [on-run-start & on-run-end](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/project-configs/on-run-start-on-run-end)
rules.remediation: Check whether the operation belongs to each model or to the whole invocation. Keep per-model work in a hook only if repeated and concurrent execution is safe. For run-level work, review every command that can invoke `on-run-start` or `on-run-end`. Use external orchestration if the operation needs a narrower execution boundary.

examples.title: Folder hook with DML
examples.bad:
models:
  demo:
    marts:
      +pre-hook: "truncate table analytics.marts.audit"
examples.good:
on-run-start:
  - "truncate table analytics.marts.audit"

rules.name: Table model rebuilds a rolling date window
rules.short_description: A table model has a relative date filter but no is_incremental() guard.
rules.long_description:
A table materialization rebuilds the rows returned by its query. If the query selects a rolling window, older rows are absent from the new table. This is valid for a deliberate rolling snapshot. It needs review if the table must retain history.

The rule reports `materialized='table'` with a relative date predicate and no `is_incremental()` call. It does not measure runtime or prove that an incremental model is cheaper.

References:
- [Materializations](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/materializations)
- [Configure incremental models](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/incremental-models)
rules.remediation: Confirm the required retention period. Keep the table model if it is a rolling snapshot. If it must retain history, consider an incremental strategy supported by the adapter. Put the incremental filter inside `is_incremental()`. Handle an empty target, equal timestamps, late rows, and backfills. Do not add a date floor that excludes required history.

examples.title: Rolling window in a table model

rules.name: Model name or config indicates a full reload
rules.short_description: The model name ends in _full_reload or _full_refresh, or full_refresh is true.
rules.long_description:
A full rebuild can be the right choice for a small model or a source with no reliable change data. A name ending in `_full_reload` or `_full_refresh` is only a naming signal; it does not control dbt. The `full_refresh: true` setting forces a full refresh for supported resources and overrides the command-line flag.

The rule reports either suffix or the setting. It does not establish that the model has outgrown full refresh.

References:
- [full_refresh](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/resource-configs/full_refresh)
- [Configure incremental models](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/incremental-models)
rules.remediation: Measure build time and confirm how source updates and deletions are captured. Use incremental processing only if it can preserve the required result. Keep a full rebuild when it is simpler or necessary, and document the reason. Review downstream references before any rename; a rename alone does not change load behavior.

examples.title: Full reload name
examples.bad:
-- models/orders_full_reload.sql
select * from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}

rules.name: Incremental model has no is_incremental() guard
rules.short_description: An incremental model has no is_incremental() call; detected stream and microbatch models are excluded.
rules.long_description:
Incremental materialization controls how dbt writes results. It does not, by itself, limit the source rows selected by the model. Without a suitable filter, each run can repeat the full transformation and merge work. Other filters or upstream change capture can still limit the input.

The rule reports an incremental model with no `is_incremental()` call. It excludes detected Snowflake stream and microbatch models. If `incremental_strategy` is unset, SSC-EWI-DBTINC0008 owns this finding instead.

Both branches must contain valid SQL. The guard is false on the first build and on an effective full refresh.

References:
- [Configure incremental models](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/incremental-models)
rules.remediation: Confirm how the source identifies changed rows. Add a guarded filter only if it captures all required changes. Handle an empty target, equal timestamps, late arrivals, and recovery after a missed run. Use a matching key for row replacement. If each run must replace all data, compare a table materialization with the current approach.

examples.title: Missing guard
examples.bad:
{{ config(materialized='incremental', unique_key='id') }}
select * from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}

rules.name: Row-replacement strategy has no unique_key
rules.short_description: An explicit merge or delete+insert strategy has no unique_key.
rules.long_description:
The `unique_key` config identifies rows to replace in common `merge` and `delete+insert` implementations. Without a key, most adapters append the selected rows, so reprocessing can create duplicates. Check the installed adapter and strategy.

The rule reports only an explicit `merge` or `delete+insert` strategy without a key. An unset strategy belongs to SSC-EWI-DBTINC0008. Append-only event data can be intentional.

A configured key does not prove that values are unique or non-null. Test the key in both the incoming data and the target.

References:
- [Configure incremental models](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/incremental-models)
- [About incremental strategy](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/incremental-strategy)
- [Add data tests to your DAG](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/data-tests)
rules.remediation: Set `unique_key` to the business key, or a list of columns that identifies one row. Add `unique` and `not_null` data tests for a single-column key. For a composite key, test the combination and each column's null handling. Resolve duplicate incoming keys before relying on merge behavior.

examples.title: Merge without a key
examples.bad:
{{ config(materialized='incremental', incremental_strategy='merge') }}
select * from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}
examples.good:
{{ config(materialized='incremental', incremental_strategy='merge', unique_key='order_id') }}
select * from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}

references.title: Add data tests to your DAG

rules.name: Incremental strategy is unset or not recognized
rules.short_description: incremental_strategy is unset or is not a built-in strategy recognized by this linter.
rules.long_description:
An omitted strategy uses the adapter default. dbt-snowflake documents `merge` as its default. An explicit setting makes the intended behavior easier to review, but does not freeze behavior across adapter upgrades.

The rule reports an unset strategy or a value outside its recognized built-in list. A custom strategy can be valid on a supported adapter and dbt version; inspect its macro before replacing it.

When the strategy is unset, this finding also covers a missing `unique_key` or `is_incremental()` guard. Verify whether the original job replaces all rows. On Snowflake, `insert_overwrite` replaces the whole table, not selected partitions.

References:
- [About incremental strategy](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/incremental-strategy)
- [Snowflake configurations](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/resource-configs/snowflake-configs)
rules.remediation: Check the installed adapter version and the intended row behavior. Use `merge` for keyed updates, `append` for new rows, or `delete+insert` for replacement of incoming keys when supported. Review custom strategies by their implementation. Test first builds, incremental runs, and full refreshes; do not choose a strategy from its name alone.

examples.title: Strategy not stated
examples.bad:
{{ config(materialized='incremental', unique_key='id') }}
select * from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}
examples.good:
{{ config(materialized='incremental', unique_key='id', incremental_strategy='merge') }}
select * from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}

rules.name: Incremental branch does not reference its target
rules.short_description: An is_incremental() branch has no target reference; detected stream and microbatch models are excluded.
rules.long_description:
The target relation can supply a watermark, such as the largest loaded change timestamp. A branch without `{{ this }}` does not use that target-based watermark. It can still use a valid rolling window or an external checkpoint.

The rule reports an `is_incremental()` branch with no `{{ this }}` reference. It excludes detected Snowflake stream and microbatch models. This is a review signal, not proof that rows are lost or reprocessed.

References:
- [Configure incremental models](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/incremental-models)
rules.remediation: Confirm how the branch selects changed rows. If a target-based watermark is appropriate, define behavior for an empty target and equal timestamps. Add a lookback only with a strategy that safely replaces reprocessed keys. Verify that the lookback covers late rows and missed runs, and provide a backfill path.

examples.title: No watermark

rules.name: Hook writes to a different relation
rules.short_description: A hook, or a macro called by a hook, writes to a relation other than the model output.
rules.long_description:
A hook can change a relation other than the model output. That write needs its own ownership, retry, and dependency rules. A hook can use `ref()` for dependencies, but the extra write is not a separate model output in the DAG.

The rule checks direct `INSERT` or `MERGE` statements against another relation. It also follows project macros called by a hook and checks their `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `MERGE`, and `DELETE` statements. Macro lookup strips a package prefix, so confirm which macro actually runs.

Per-model audit logging can be intentional. Do not change it to once-per-run logging without checking the required records.

References:
- [pre-hook & post-hook](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/resource-configs/pre-hook-post-hook)
- [on-run-start & on-run-end](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/project-configs/on-run-start-on-run-end)
- [Materializations](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/materializations)
- [About ref function](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/dbt-jinja-functions/ref)
rules.remediation: Make a separate dbt model when the target is a transformation output. For audit or control data, document the writer and retry behavior. Move work to `on-run-end` only if it belongs to the whole invocation and is safe for every command that runs that hook.

examples.title: Hook writes another table
examples.bad:
{{ config(post_hook='insert into audit.load_log select 1') }}
select * from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}
examples.good:
-- models/audit/load_log.sql is its own dbt model
select 1 as load_id

rules.name: Merge exclusion names a column not found in the model
rules.short_description: A merge_exclude_columns entry is not found in the model SQL.
rules.long_description:
The `merge_exclude_columns` config prevents updates to selected columns on matched rows. It does not provide values for new rows. If a listed column is absent from the model output, inspect the compiled merge and schema handling. The result can be an error or a missing value; it is not always NULL.

The rule uses column-name text checks, not a resolved output schema. It skips a model when a detected macro call could generate the column list. A star projection can also require manual review.

References:
- [About incremental strategy](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/incremental-strategy)
- [Configure incremental models](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/incremental-models)
rules.remediation: Check the compiled output columns and the adapter's merge behavior. Select the excluded column with the intended insert-time value if the model owns it. Otherwise, remove the stale exclusion only after checking defaults, schema changes, and existing data. Test both inserts and updates.

examples.title: Excluded column not selected
examples.bad:
{{ config(materialized='incremental', unique_key='id', incremental_strategy='merge', merge_exclude_columns=['created_at']) }}
select id, amount from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}
examples.good:
{{ config(materialized='incremental', unique_key='id', incremental_strategy='merge', merge_exclude_columns=['created_at']) }}
select id, amount, current_timestamp() as created_at from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}

rules.name: Append model contains possible change-tracking columns
rules.short_description: An append model includes names such as updated_at, status, or valid_to.
rules.long_description:
The `append` strategy inserts rows without replacing existing rows or checking for duplicates. If the source restates the current version of a record, repeated runs can add more versions of that key. An event or history model can intentionally retain these versions.

The rule reports `append` with column names that suggest mutable data, such as `updated_at`, `status`, or `valid_to`. Names alone do not prove that an update strategy is needed.

References:
- [About incremental strategy](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/incremental-strategy)
rules.remediation: Define the model's row grain. For one current row per business key, consider a supported keyed replacement strategy such as `merge`. For an append-only event or history model, document the version key and how consumers select records. Test retries so they do not add unintended duplicates.

examples.title: Append with updated_at
examples.bad:
{{ config(materialized='incremental', incremental_strategy='append') }}
select id, status, updated_at from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}
examples.good:
{{ config(materialized='incremental', incremental_strategy='merge', unique_key='id') }}
select id, status, updated_at from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}

rules.name: Target-based incremental filter has no date floor
rules.short_description: An incremental branch references its target but has no date bound recognized by the rule.
rules.long_description:
Snowflake does not use a predicate with a subquery for micro-partition pruning, even when the subquery returns a constant. A separate date bound can help, but only if it preserves every required row. Check the query profile before adding one.

The rule reports a target-referencing incremental branch without a recognized date expression, date literal, or `var()` call. This is a text check, not proof of a full scan. Detected Snowflake stream and microbatch models are excluded.

An `is_incremental()` filter does not run on the first build or an effective full refresh. A floor inside that branch cannot reduce those initial scans.

References:
- [Micro-partitions & Data Clustering](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/tables-clustering-micropartitions)
- [Configure incremental models](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/incremental-models)
rules.remediation: Measure the incremental scan. Add a separate date bound only when the source's lateness and recovery requirements permit it. Make the bound adjustable for missed runs and backfills. Do not use the seven-day example as a universal setting: it can exclude required rows after a long outage. Keep first-build and full-refresh history requirements explicit.

examples.title: Watermark without a floor

rules.name: External loader may write to a dbt model
rules.short_description: A task or procedure writes to a relation name that matches a dbt model.
rules.long_description:
A task or procedure that writes to the same relation as dbt creates two writers. A later rebuild can remove those rows, and concurrent writes can change the result of tests. The exact effect depends on the materialization and execution order.

The rule looks for writes in task or procedure SQL and matches the target's final name to a model name. Confirm the database, schema, alias, and quoting before treating the match as shared ownership.

A relation maintained outside dbt can be declared as a source so dbt records its downstream dependencies.

References:
- [Materializations](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/materializations)
- [Add sources to your DAG](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/sources)
rules.remediation: Confirm that both writers target the same relation. Choose one owner. Move the transformation into a dbt model if dbt should own the result. If an external job owns it, remove the competing dbt writer and declare the relation as a source. Coordinate the change with the loader schedule and consumers.

examples.title: Procedure loads a dbt model
examples.good: -- Remove the procedure. The dbt model `orders` owns the load.

rules.name: Pre-hook updates the model's own relation
rules.short_description: A pre-hook updates the model relation before the materialization runs.
rules.long_description:
A pre-hook update changes rows before dbt builds the model. If the update commits separately and the build fails, the changed rows remain without the intended follow-up work. Transaction behavior differs by adapter; do not assume a shared hook transaction on Snowflake.

The rule reports `UPDATE {{ this }}` in a model pre-hook or an inherited folder pre-hook. Retain the hook only after confirming that repeated execution and failed runs are safe.

References:
- [pre-hook & post-hook](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/resource-configs/pre-hook-post-hook)
- [About incremental strategy](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/incremental-strategy)
rules.remediation: Check which rows and values the pre-hook changes. If keyed replacement expresses the same operation, return the changed rows from the model and use a supported `merge` strategy with `unique_key`. Test inserts, updates, retries, and failures. Do not assume that changing strategies creates one transaction for every adapter.

examples.title: Update leg as a pre-hook
examples.bad:
{{ config(pre_hook="update {{ this }} set status = 'closed' where id in (select id from {{ ref('closed') }})") }}
select * from {{ ref('orders') }}
examples.good:
{{ config(materialized='incremental', unique_key='id', incremental_strategy='merge') }}
select id, 'closed' as status from {{ ref('closed') }}

rules.name: Hook reads a model that overrides an ephemeral default
rules.short_description: A hook references a view or table model whose folder default is ephemeral.
rules.long_description:
An ephemeral model becomes a CTE in a dependent model query; it has no standalone database relation. A hook that needs to query a stored relation can therefore require a view or table.

The rule reports a view or table that overrides an ephemeral folder default and appears in another model hook's `ref()` call. This does not prove that the hook caused the override or that the override is wrong. Keep the stored relation when it is needed for the hook, other readers, or measured performance.

References:
- [Materializations](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/materializations)
- [pre-hook & post-hook](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/resource-configs/pre-hook-post-hook)
rules.remediation: Check why the hook needs the relation. Move the read into model SQL only if that preserves the operation's timing and result. Then consider ephemeral materialization if no consumer needs direct access. Otherwise, keep the view or table and document the reason for the override.

examples.title: Hook reads an intermediate
examples.bad: {{ config(pre_hook="{{ count_rows(ref('int_x')) }}") }}  -- int_x forced to view
examples.good: -- compute the count in the model body; int_x stays ephemeral

rules.name: Hook exports data to stage files
rules.short_description: A hook runs COPY INTO a stage, directly or through a macro.
rules.long_description:
`COPY INTO` a stage exports query results to files. A hook can perform this export, but the files are not a separate dbt model output. An export in a model post-hook can run before later tests or other models fail.

The rule reports `COPY INTO @...` in a hook or a macro called by the hook. This local review policy does not mean dbt forbids unload hooks. Review file naming, retries, and the condition that makes an export ready for consumers.

References:
- [Data unloading considerations](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/data-unload-considerations)
- [pre-hook & post-hook](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/resource-configs/pre-hook-post-hook)
- [on-run-start & on-run-end](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/project-configs/on-run-start-on-run-end)
- [About dbt build command](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/commands/build)
rules.remediation: If consumers require tested results, run the export from orchestration only after the required `dbt build` succeeds. If using `on-run-end`, inspect run results before exporting and account for every command that invokes the hook. Define safe retries and output publication. Moving the hook alone does not guarantee a complete, validated export.

examples.title: Post-hook unload
examples.bad: {{ config(post_hook="copy into @out/orders from {{ this }}") }}
examples.good: -- run COPY INTO from orchestration after dbt build

rules.name: Hook SQL comes from a runtime variable
rules.short_description: A hook gets its SQL from var(), so command-line variables can change the executed statement.
rules.long_description:
A hook can get SQL directly from `var()` or from a variable assigned by `var()`. The `--vars` argument can override project defaults. Review must therefore include the caller's values, not only the model text. This mechanism is valid dbt behavior, but unrestricted SQL overrides can execute statements that were not reviewed.

The rule reports these variable-fed hooks. Model `config()` hooks are grouped into one finding per project, with affected paths in `context.files`.

Accept the pattern only when the caller and permitted statements are controlled and documented. It does not inherently bypass dbt compilation or tests.

References:
- [Project variables](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/project-variables)
- [pre-hook & post-hook](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/resource-configs/pre-hook-post-hook)
rules.remediation: Inspect the orchestration arguments before changing a variable. Converted jobs may depend on runtime overrides. If no caller supplies a value, confirm the default behavior before replacing the variable read. If callers supply values, preserve required behavior and document the caller, permitted statements, and tests. Prefer a reviewed macro with bounded inputs where practical.

examples.title: Hook from var
examples.bad:
{% set pre_sql = var('k_pre_sql', '') %}
{% if pre_sql != '' %}{{ config(pre_hook=pre_sql) }}{% endif %}
examples.good: {{ config(pre_hook="{{ my_reviewed_macro() }}") }}

rules.name: Hook scope may differ from the orchestration scope
rules.short_description: A hook macro uses raw variable_scope where orchestration may use a run-prefixed scope.
rules.long_description:
A control-table write and read must use the same scope value. A raw scope will not match a run-prefixed scope when the prefix is nonempty. Jinja's `~` operator concatenates strings; the exact scope format is defined by the migrated application, not by dbt.

The rule looks for `variable_scope = '{{ variable_scope }}'` in a hook-called macro that touches a control table. It reports warning when project orchestration SQL contains `GetRunScopePrefix() ||`; otherwise it reports information.

This is a local migration convention check. The cited Jinja documentation explains concatenation, not the application-specific prefix contract. No change is needed if both sides deliberately use the same unprefixed scope.

References:
- [Template Designer Documentation: Other Operators](https://jinja.palletsprojects.com/en/stable/templates/#other-operators)
- [pre-hook & post-hook](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/resource-configs/pre-hook-post-hook)
rules.remediation: Trace the scope value from orchestration into the hook. Use the same construction on reads and writes, and apply a run prefix exactly once. Test two concurrent runs and a retry. Preserve the existing convention unless the mismatch is confirmed; do not create a prefix function solely because the example names one.

examples.title: Raw scope in macro
examples.bad: update control_variables set variable_value = 1 where variable_scope = '{{ variable_scope }}'
examples.good: update control_variables set variable_value = 1 where variable_scope = '{{ run_scope_prefix() ~ variable_scope }}'

rules.name: Incremental and full branches select different columns
rules.short_description: The is_incremental() branch and its else branch have different select lists.
rules.long_description:
Different select lists can produce different schemas on the first build and later incremental runs. Whether the model succeeds depends on the adapter, target schema, and `on_schema_change` setting. Schema-change settings do not backfill new columns in old rows.

The rule compares select lists in an `is_incremental()` branch and its else branch. A star in either branch skips the check. Equal lists are not reported. The check does not prove that data types or values match.

References:
- [Configure incremental models](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/incremental-models)
rules.remediation: Keep the output columns and types consistent when only the row filter needs to change. Put that filter inside `is_incremental()`. If the schema difference is deliberate, verify `on_schema_change`, required backfills, and adapter support. Test the first build, incremental run, and full refresh separately.

examples.title: Different column lists
examples.bad: {% if is_incremental() %}select id, a from t{% else %}select id, b from t{% endif %}
examples.good:
select id, a from t
{% if is_incremental() %}where a > (select max(a) from {{ this }}){% endif %}
